md: Anchors and grid cells are not predictions. They are fixed reference positions that predictions are expressed relative to. A detector with 20000 anchors does not find 20000 objects; almost all of them are scored as background.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
md: S3 is not just a slow disk. A disk charges nothing per write and lets you overwrite 4 KiB in place. S3 charges per request, writes whole immutable objects, and takes tens to a couple of hundred milliseconds per request. Every design in this course reshapes writes into **few, large, immutable objects**.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
md: Counts aggregate; quantiles do not. If you want to compute a percentile across instances, regions or time windows later, you must store counts per bucket now. That single decision is why histograms beat summaries almost everywhere.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Finding text: EAST geometry maps and DBNet's learnable threshold
md: Dense text detectors predict a per-pixel map. EAST regresses a box from every text pixel and merges them; DBNet segments shrunk text kernels with a learned threshold, then expands them back.

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: The reference monitor: one checker that sees every access
md: "We check permissions in the web UI" is not complete mediation. If the API behind the UI, a batch job or a debug endpoint reaches the same data without the check, the monitor is bypassed. Ask of every design: is there any path to the object that skips the checker?

courseTitle: OS security, privilege and isolation
lessonTitle: Virtual machines, containers, gVisor and Firecracker
md: Containers share the host kernel; their strength is the strength of that kernel plus the filters in front of it. VMs give each workload its own kernel and put a small VMM on the boundary. gVisor puts a memory-safe kernel of its own in between. Choose by how untrusted the code is: your own services, other teams' code, or strangers' code.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
md: A green local run does not prove CI will pass. CI tests your change merged into the latest base branch, on a clean machine, often across several OS and Python versions. Read the workflow file to see what will actually run.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: What a reviewer is deciding: the code-health standard
md: Approve when the change makes the codebase better than it was, not when it matches what you would have written. There is no perfect code, only better code. The goal is continuous improvement.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Where a project's rules live and how GitHub finds them
md: A repository with no `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its file list may still have one. It can be in `.github/` or `docs/`, or inherited from the organization's `.github` repository, which never shows up in the repository's own files or clone. Use the link GitHub shows on the new issue or PR page.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Fork, clone and two remotes: origin and upstream
md: Fetch from `upstream`, push to `origin`. Remote-tracking branches like `upstream/main` are snapshots from your last fetch, not live views.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Sign-off, the DCO, and how your commits land upstream
md: `-s` adds a Signed-off-by trailer whose meaning the project defines (often the DCO). Read CONTRIBUTING to learn whether the project wants sign-offs, fixups squashed, and which merge method it uses.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
md: A sign-off you add without reading the DCO is still a legal statement about provenance. Copying code you cannot trace (a gist without a license, generated output in a project that bans it) and signing off is exactly what the DCO exists to prevent.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Regression checks: perf bots and noise thresholds from history
md: Regression checks only work if noise is known. A bot learns each benchmark's normal spread from history and flags changes beyond it; you do the same by hand with repeated, interleaved runs and a test.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
md: "Same problem" means the *same* failure, not just any failure. If removing a line turns a `StatisticsError` into a `NameError`, you did not shrink the bug; you created a new one. Compare the exception type and message every time, not just whether something crashed.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
md: Misconception: "small" means "tiny". Google's guide also says a change can be too small to understand: if you add a new API, include a use of it in the same change so reviewers can judge it.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
md: The block table is the whole trick: contiguous logical blocks, scattered physical blocks, allocation on demand. Waste is capped at one partly filled block per sequence.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Authorisation: scope, rules of engagement and permission
md: If something is not written in the scope, it is out of scope. When a new system appears mid-test (a subdomain, an extra address range), stop and get written approval to add it. PTES names scope creep as a common failure, especially during retesting.

courseTitle: Penetration testing methodology and recon
lessonTitle: Reporting: from finding to fix, and the retest
md: A finding is done when the client can understand it, verify it safely, fix the cause as well as the symptom, and see it marked closed after a retest.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
md: The workflow: record with a modest rate and working stacks, fold, filter, draw, read top edges, fix the widest plateau that you can change, then measure again.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: The persuasion levers every lure pulls
md: Misconception: "spotting bad grammar catches phishing". Spelling mistakes were never the core of a lure, and well-written messages are now easy to produce: the FBI's 2025 IC3 report notes businesses reported over USD 30 million in losses to BEC scams involving AI. Train on the levers and the process rules, not on typos.

courseTitle: Phishing, social engineering and email security
lessonTitle: Layered defences and the analyst workflow for a reported phish
md: The NCSC also warns that punishing people for clicking simulated phish erodes trust and stops them reporting real mistakes; it starts to resemble entrapment. Teach the levers and process rules (lesson 2), make reporting effortless, and celebrate reports.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Rust layout: default repr, repr(C), and niches
md: C keeps your field order and you are responsible for packing it well. Rust's default repr may reorder fields and use niches to save space, but promises no exact layout. Use `#[repr(C)]` whenever bytes cross a boundary your compiler does not control.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Post-filtering: why top-k comes back short
md: Post-filtering leaves the index untouched and is cheap when $s$ is large, but the result count is a random variable. To hold k results you must fetch on the order of $k/s$ candidates, and noticeably more for a high-probability guarantee.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Software prefetch: distance, hints and the kernel's lesson
md: **Rule:** add a software prefetch only where profiling shows misses, one site at a time, and keep it only if performance counters (hardware registers in the CPU that count events such as cache misses and prefetches, read with tools like perf) show useful prefetches and the timing improves. Drepper and the kernel developers reached the same conclusion from opposite results.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Location traces and aggregate maps: Strava 2018
md: "It's only aggregate data" fails when the crowd is small. A count of 25 is not one person, but it is 25 identifiable people at a place they did not mean to reveal.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: The Laplace mechanism: calibrating noise, worked
md: Laplace mechanism: add noise with scale sensitivity / epsilon. For counts that is 1 / epsilon, and 95 percent of answers fall within about 3 / epsilon of the truth. Every query spends epsilon from a finite budget.

courseTitle: Privacy engineering: re-identification, differential privacy, PETs
lessonTitle: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them
md: PSI reveals set sizes and the intersection, and it cannot stop a party from choosing what goes into its own set. Cap sizes, rate-limit, and log query volumes per client to detect enumeration.

courseTitle: Privilege escalation and lateral movement
lessonTitle: After the foothold: the four tactics defenders must see
md: The foothold is rarely the disaster. Escalation, credential theft, discovery and lateral movement turn one infected laptop into a domain-wide incident, and each of them leaves evidence on the machines it touches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Distances from codes: lookup tables, SDC and ADC
md: ADC = exact query, quantized database. Per query you build an $m \times k^*$ table once, then each database vector costs $m$ lookups and adds. This is why PQ scans are fast and why everyone uses ADC.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Sequence recovery is a proxy, not a goal. A design that recovers 100 percent of a natural sequence has designed nothing new, and a design that recovers 30 percent may fold perfectly well. Recovery is useful only because it correlates with getting the physics right. What you actually test is whether the designed sequence folds back to the backbone you asked for.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Files, functions and exceptions: scripts that survive bad input
md: Read files with `with open(..., encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")`, put reusable steps in functions, and catch only the exceptions you can handle. A missing log is a finding, not a zero.

courseTitle: Python for security work: parsing, automating and calling APIs
lessonTitle: Safe coding habits: no eval, no shell strings, no secrets in code
md: Data is never code. Parse it with a format-specific parser, pass it to other programs as list arguments, validate it against what it should be, and keep secrets in the environment, not in the file.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
md: Misconception: the rewriter should make the query richer. Its job is to make it *standalone and faithful*. A rewriter that adds guessed facts (say, "when the leader fails during a network partition") can steer retrieval toward documents the user never asked about. Instruct it not to answer, and to return the message unchanged when it is already standalone.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
md: Per vector, the query-time work is a few AND plus popcount passes over the D-bit code and a handful of multiply-adds with precomputed factors. The error bound then tells you which candidates are worth an exact distance.

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Race conditions from zero: concurrency, the race window and TOCTOU
md: A lock inside one process (threading.Lock here) protects only threads in that process. A web app with several worker processes or servers needs the lock where the state lives, usually in the database (lesson 9).

courseTitle: Race conditions and business logic flaws
lessonTitle: Why "too fast to exploit" fails: jitter and the single-packet attack
md: The single-packet attack made network distance irrelevant: a tester far away can now hit a 1 ms window about as reliably as one on the same network. Treat every check-then-act as reachable, and fix it with atomicity, not with speed.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft log replication: AppendEntries, nextIndex and commit
md: Stored on a majority is not the same as committed. An entry from an *earlier* term can sit on a majority and still be erased by a later leader. Commitment is only decided by counting replicas of an entry from the leader's *current* term, which then commits everything before it.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: What a ranker sees: one feature vector per query-document pair
md: A ranking model only knows what its feature vector tells it. If a signal that decides relevance (freshness for news, location for local search) is not encoded as a number for each query-document pair, no amount of model tuning can recover it.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: ERR: a user who stops once satisfied
md: **$g_{\max}$ is a convention, and tools hard-code it.** TREC's `gdeval.pl` (the official Web track script, which ir_measures used for `ERR@5` in our test) sets `MAX_JUDGMENT = 4`. With our 0 to 3 grades, gdeval gives Run A an ERR@5 of 0.240, not 0.452, and Run B 0.438, not 0.875. Rankings of runs may survive, but the numbers cannot be compared with an ERR computed under $g_{\max} = 3$.

courseTitle: Ransomware: how the business works, and how to resist and recover
lessonTitle: Case: Change Healthcare and ALPHV, February 2024
md: One remote access portal without MFA, at one subsidiary, gave a criminal nine quiet days. Inventory every remote access path (VPNs, Citrix, RDP gateways, vendor portals, acquired companies' systems) and enforce MFA on all of them, then test that it is enforced.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
md: An (address, rkey) pair is a capability: whoever holds it, on a QP in the same protection domain, can read or write that memory with no further check by your CPU. Grant the narrowest access flags you need, and revoke by deregistering (`ibv_dereg_mr`) or with memory windows, which the manual describes as a cheaper way to grant and revoke remote access dynamically.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Client-side prediction and server reconciliation
md: Each server state is a statement about the past: "here is the world after your input #n". Reset to it, then replay inputs after #n. Sequence numbers are what make that subtraction possible.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Two-stage systems: candidate generation, two towers, ranking
md: Retrieval must be cheap per item (dot products over precomputed vectors); ranking can be expensive per item. In-batch negatives are sampled by popularity, so correct each logit by log p_j.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: A query plan is a tree of operators that pull rows
md: Cost units are not milliseconds. They are relative estimates the planner uses to compare plans. To see real time, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE, which actually runs the query.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leader replication: when is a commit really safe?
md: A commit is only as safe as the set of machines that had it when the client was told "ok". Every replication knob is a choice of *how many* and *which* machines that set must include, paid for in commit latency.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: KL regularization: a leash, not a cure
md: KL regularization and early stopping limit the *amount* of optimization, which keeps you on the rising side of the Goodhart curve. They cannot tell a good high-reward behavior from a bad one. Only a better reward, a conservative reward, or an outside check can do that.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Monte Carlo: simulating 100,000 years of losses
md: Monte Carlo is not magic: garbage ranges give precise-looking garbage. The model also assumes the factors are independent (here, a bad attack year does not make secondary losses bigger), which may not hold. Show your inputs with the outputs, say what is assumed, and rerun when estimates change. Simplified: real FAIR tools also model multiple loss forms separately and correlations between factors.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: ISO/IEC 27001: an ISMS, Annex A and the certification audit
md: ISO 27001 certifies a management system: risk assessment, treatment, a Statement of Applicability against 93 Annex A controls, internal audit, management review, continual improvement. Certificates last three years with yearly surveillance. The SoA and your risk register are the documents everything else hangs from.

courseTitle: Risk, governance and compliance for engineers
lessonTitle: Breach notification clocks and US disclosure rules
md: Know your clocks before the incident: NIS2 24 h and 72 h, GDPR 72 h from awareness, SEC four business days from a materiality decision made without unreasonable delay, state laws often 30 to 60 days, HIPAA at most 60 days. Encryption is an exemption almost everywhere. Prepare templates and decision owners in the incident plan.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: Rollout is the bottleneck. FLOPs are dominated by training, but wall-clock time is dominated by sequential decoding. Most RL infrastructure ideas (fast inference engines, placement, resharding, asynchrony, partial rollouts) are ways to make generation faster or to keep the other GPUs busy while it runs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100, NVIDIA's 2017 data center GPU (125 TFLOP/s of Tensor Core math over about 900 GB/s, a ridge of 138.9), to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: C calls Rust: a misc device from open() to ioctl()
md: Direction matters at the boundary: Rust calling C uses `to_result`/`from_err_ptr`; C calling Rust uses a trampoline that returns `err.to_errno()`. Ownership crossing the boundary goes through `into_foreign` once and `from_foreign` once.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: The scheduling cycle: select_cpu, enqueue, dispatch, run
md: Stashing a task in a BPF map from `select_cpu` does not skip `enqueue`; only a DSQ insertion does. The docs call storing tasks from `select_cpu` racy and discouraged. Also, the core ignores an invalid CPU choice such as one outside the task's allowed cpumask (the set of CPUs a task may run on, set with `sched_setaffinity()`).

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Keeping tasks in BPF: custody, dequeue and user-space policy
md: Misconception: once a task is in a custom DSQ it is on its way to a CPU. It is in your custody until dispatch moves it, and a property change can pull it back out through `ops.dequeue()` at any time.

courseTitle: Secrets and key management
lessonTitle: Vaults: one place to store, control and audit secrets
md: A vault concentrates risk. CircleCI was, in effect, a vault for its customers' deploy secrets. Narrow policies per workload, short-lived tokens, audit logs shipped elsewhere, the ability to seal fast, and a root of trust in a KMS or HSM are what make the concentration worth it.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Taint by hand: following one value from source to sink
md: Trace by hand: mark the source, follow every assignment and call, and stop at each sink. A function only counts as a sanitizer if its output is safe for that specific sink, whatever the input. Rewriting or deleting bad patterns almost never qualifies.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Log4Shell as a review miss: a logger that interpreted its input
md: Parameterising user data protects you only if the component never interprets the final string. When reviewing a feature that adds interpretation (lookups, templates, expressions, fetching URLs) to a widely used API, treat every caller's data as reaching that new sink.

courseTitle: Secure code review: spot the bug in Python, Go, JS, C and Rust
lessonTitle: Memory-safe roadmaps: CISA's guidance and Android's numbers
md: Memory-safety policy is now a review topic: new memory-unsafe code needs a reason, unsafe blocks in Rust get the most scrutiny, and old C and C++ keeps its hardening. Android's data says the payoff comes from new code, because vulnerabilities concentrate in recent changes.

courseTitle: Secure network protocols: IPsec, WireGuard, SSH, RADIUS and friends
lessonTitle: SSH's transport layer: version, KEXINIT, key exchange and host keys
md: Everything in the KEXINIT lists is negotiated in the clear and only later authenticated through the exchange hash. Anything the hash does not cover (extra messages, the implicit sequence numbers) is a place where an active attacker can interfere.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Biba and integrity: no read down, no write up
md: Confidentiality: no read up, no write down. Integrity: no read down, no write up. If you remember which way information is allowed to flow, you can rebuild both rule sets.

courseTitle: Security architecture and zero trust
lessonTitle: Identity-aware proxies and ZTNA versus the VPN
md: A proxy only protects an application if it is the only way in and the application can tell the difference. Signed, audience-bound assertions let the application check for itself.

courseTitle: Security automation and AI-assisted security operations
lessonTitle: Rate limits, backoff with jitter, and partial failure
md: Pace all workers with one shared limiter, honour Retry-After and the reset headers, back off exponentially with full jitter, retry only idempotent calls and only at one layer, and report partial failures item by item.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: What security protects: assets and the CIA triad
md: A hash only proves integrity if the expected fingerprint reached you over a channel the attacker cannot touch. If an attacker can change both the message and the published hash, the check passes. Fixing that needs authenticity: a digital signature (or a keyed hash) that only the real sender can produce. The cryptography course covers these.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: Scoring and prioritising: CVSS, KEV and EPSS
md: CVSS = how bad in theory. KEV = being used now. EPSS = likely to be used soon. Combine them with what *your* asset is and how exposed it is. A score without context is not a priority.

courseTitle: Security from zero: assets, threats, vulnerabilities and exploits
lessonTitle: The legal and ethical line: authorisation and disclosure
md: Rules of thumb that keep you on the right side: test only systems you own or have written permission to test; stay inside the agreed scope (systems, dates, methods); stop and report the moment you see other people's data; never keep or share it. A bug bounty programme's published rules are a form of written permission, but only for what they list.

courseTitle: Writing and influence for security work
lessonTitle: Getting a fix shipped when you cannot order it
md: Escalation is not a weapon. If owners learn that talking to security means being reported upward, they stop talking to security, and you lose the early warnings that matter most. Agree the path in advance, use it predictably, and make the first step always a direct conversation.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
md: For any self-improvement claim, ask two questions: what outside the current model decides that a sample is good, and how often is it wrong? The loop can only improve as far as that signal is informative.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: Why cloud metadata is the prize: Capital One 2019
md: Two failures made one breach. The SSRF (a WAF that relayed requests inward) gave a single credential read. The **over-permissioned role** (a firewall that could list and read every bucket) turned that read into 100 million records. Least privilege on the role would have made the same SSRF far less damaging.

courseTitle: Server-side attacks: SSRF, deserialization, XXE and file handling
lessonTitle: When front end and back end disagree: smuggling and ProxyLogon
md: Whenever one server forwards to another, ask two questions: do both agree on what the request *is* (its boundaries, its host, its path), and does the back end trust the front end's identity for actions the original user was never allowed to do?

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Dijkstra's algorithm: settle nodes in order of distance
md: Common misconception: Dijkstra "heads toward" the target. It does not look at the target at all until it pops it. It settles every node closer than t, in all directions, which on a road map is a disc around s whose radius is the trip length.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
md: Zero-padding does not improve resolution. Smith: padding a 256-point signal to 2048 points gives 1025 spectrum samples, but "the added zeros don't change the shape of the spectrum, they only provide more samples in the frequency domain." To separate two close frequencies you need a longer *recording*.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Masks instead of branches: compares, blends and AVX-512
md: Lanes cannot branch, so SIMD code computes both sides, builds a per-lane mask with a compare, and selects. AVX2 keeps masks in vector registers and uses blendv and movemask; AVX-512 has mask registers k0 to k7 with merge or zero masking, which also handles loop tails.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
md: Slab = one cache per object size or type, slabs of whole pages cut into equal objects, a refcount per slab for trivial reclaim, and objects kept constructed between uses. It removes most of both internal and external fragmentation for small, frequent objects.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Async in slime means: same train.py, different rollout function, separate GPU pools. You trade a bounded amount of policy staleness for not waiting on the slowest trajectory.

courseTitle: Security operations: alert triage and investigation
lessonTitle: Malware on an endpoint: reading a process tree
md: A process tree shows execution, not intent. Developer tools, installers and IT scripts produce strange trees every day. The tree tells you where to look; the evidence on each node (path, signer, command line, network) decides the verdict.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: Security is a secondary task: why people work around it
md: Every security control spends someone's time and attention. Spend it where it buys the most risk reduction, automate the rest, and treat widespread workarounds as evidence that the control is badly designed.

courseTitle: Social engineering, human factors and physical security
lessonTitle: What a lock really does: pin tumblers, master keys and key control
md: Keys are bearer tokens with no audit trail and no revocation. Keep master keys rare and inventoried, re-key when keys go missing or holders leave, and put rooms whose access you need to prove or revoke behind electronic access control with logs.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Enforcing sparsity: L1, TopK and JumpReLU
md: TopK fixes L0 = k on every token, even when a token needs more or fewer features. JumpReLU and L1 SAEs let L0 vary, so their reported L0 is an average over tokens.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: The semivariogram: measuring how similarity decays with distance
md: An empirical variogram from a handful of points is very noisy, and the fitted range and nugget can swing a lot with the bin edges or the fitting weights. Look at the plot, try a second binning and treat the parameters as uncertain, not as measured truths.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Draft, verify, keep: the loop with greedy decoding
md: A common bug: after a rejection, keeping the target's distributions for later positions. Those were computed with the rejected guess in the context, so they condition on a token that is no longer in the output. Only the distribution at the first rejected position is valid.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
md: Whisper is an audio-conditioned language model. The encoder turns 30 s of log-mel into 1500 vectors; the decoder generates the transcript token by token, with language, task and timestamps expressed as tokens in the same sequence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
md: Stack memory lives exactly as long as the function call that created it. Allocation and release are a pointer adjustment, which is why the size must be bounded and why anything that must outlive the call has to go somewhere else: the heap.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: TLB reach = entries x page size. Working sets beyond it pay a page walk on most random accesses; huge pages raise reach by 512 times, and every unmap in a multithreaded process may interrupt other CPUs.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Positional encoding and the full encoder-decoder stack
md: "Attention is all you need" does not mean attention is all there is. Without the FFN, residual connections, normalization and positional encodings, a stack of attention layers loses most of its parameters, its sense of order, and its trainability.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
md: Saturation does not mean repeated terms are ignored. With k1 = 1.2, going from 1 to 2 occurrences still raises the factor from 0.45 to 0.62. It means each extra occurrence is worth less than the one before, with a hard ceiling.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Stacking blocks: residuals, pre-LayerNorm, MLP and a tied output head
md: Pre-LN vs post-LN is not cosmetic. Xiong et al. show that in the original post-LN Transformer the gradients near the output are large at initialization, which is why it needs a careful learning-rate warmup. Placing LayerNorm inside the residual branch, as GPT-2 does, gives well-behaved gradients at initialization.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: A derivative is the slope you see when you zoom in
md: $f'(x)$ answers: if I nudge $x$ by a tiny amount, how many times that amount does $f$ change? Positive means $f$ rises to the right, negative means it falls, zero means the tangent is flat.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: The gradient gives the direction; the learning rate decides the distance. The largest stable learning rate is set by the **steepest** direction of the loss, while progress in the **shallowest** direction decides how long training takes.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
md: A command runs in a **copy** of the shell. It inherits open files, the working directory and exported variables, and nothing it changes flows back. Only builtins and functions run inside the shell itself.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: files, scripts, pipes and ssh
lessonTitle: Searching and transforming text: grep, regex, find, sed and awk
md: grep selects lines, sed rewrites them, awk computes over fields, and find selects files. Single-quote every pattern so the shell leaves it alone, and add `-E` when you want `+`, `?`, `|` or groups.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: From one-hot IDs to a trainable embedding table
md: An embedding is a learned weight matrix indexed by item ID. Meaning is not built in: the vectors start random and become useful only because some training objective rewards putting related items close together. The rest of this course is about which objectives do that.

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: Contrastive training in practice: in-batch negatives and collapse
md: A falling contrastive loss is not proof of a good representation: a model can solve the training task with features that transfer poorly, as SimCLR's normalization ablation shows. Track a downstream measure such as linear evaluation, and check for collapse by looking at the spread of the embeddings.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Batching: sharing each weight read across many users
md: Decode is memory-bound, so throughput comes from making every weight read serve many tokens. Batch size is capped by KV-cache memory, and continuous batching keeps that batch full as requests come and go.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Decisions in machine code: flags, compare and conditional jumps
md: An `if` is a compare that sets flags plus a conditional jump that reads them. Signed and unsigned comparisons differ only in which flags the jump reads: SF and OF for signed (jl, jg), CF for unsigned (jb, ja).

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: Reward models: turning human comparisons into a score
md: A reward model is a learned approximation, not ground truth. Stiennon et al. (2020), an OpenAI paper that used RLHF to summarize Reddit posts, found their reward model preferred longer summaries, and it can be confidently wrong on responses unlike its training data. Lesson 9 shows what happens when RL optimizes hard against such a model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Building the index: tokens, sorting and postings
md: Whatever normalization you apply at index time (lowercasing, stemming, stripping punctuation) you must apply identically to queries. If the index stores `cache` and the query parser passes `Cache` through unchanged, the dictionary lookup finds nothing.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: C in one sitting: types, operators, control flow and functions
md: `sum / 10` with an int sum is integer division: 38, not 38.5. Convert one operand first, `(double)sum / 10`. A *cast* `(type)expr` converts a value to the named type.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: Off by one is the classic C bug: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;` writes a[n], one element past the end. The loop condition for an n-element array is `i < n`. Neither the compiler nor the CPU checks array bounds for you.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Function pointers and void *: writing generic code like qsort
md: qsort passes pointers **to elements**, not the elements. For an array of `item`, each argument is really an `item *`. For an array of strings declared `const char *words[]`, each element is itself a pointer, so the argument is a pointer to a pointer: `strcmp(*(const char * const *)a, *(const char * const *)b)`. Casting to the wrong type compiles silently and compares garbage.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Rust for C programmers: cargo, let, structs, enums and match
md: Rust's types carry what C leaves to convention: `Option<T>` instead of NULL, `Result<T, E>` instead of -1 and errno, exhaustive `match` so no case is forgotten, and `let` immutable unless you write `mut`. Ownership, next, does the same for *who frees this*.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Ownership in methods and loops: self, &self, &mut self and for
md: `.clone()` makes most of these errors disappear, but for E0507 a borrow (`&v[0]`) is usually what you meant. Clone only when you need an independent String that outlives the Vec or changes separately from it.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: Adding vectors of different dimensions is undefined in math. NumPy and PyTorch will sometimes *broadcast* (silently repeat) a smaller array to fit, so shape bugs can produce a result instead of an error. Always know the shape of every array you add. The tensors lesson gives the exact rule.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Determinant and inverse: undoing a map and solving Ax = b
md: A tiny determinant does not by itself mean trouble. $0.1I$ in 10 dimensions has determinant $10^{-10}$ yet condition number 1: it shrinks every direction equally and is trivial to undo. Ill-conditioning is about *unequal* stretching, which the condition number (and the SVD lesson) measures.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Linear layers are batched dot products ($XW^\top + b$). Attention scores are dot products between queries and keys ($QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$). Similarity search is a matrix-vector product. Vectors, dot products and matrix multiplication cover all three.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Classification end to end: logistic regression, boundaries and softmax
md: Logistic regression scores $z = w \cdot x + b$, squashes with the sigmoid, and learns from the gradient $(p - y)x$. Its decision boundary is the line $z = 0$. Softmax generalizes it to K classes with gradient $p - \text{onehot}(y)$. On separable data, weights grow without bound unless you regularize.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Measuring a model: metrics, thresholds and cross-validation
md: Choose metrics that match the costs: precision and recall for rare positives, AUC for ranking, RMSE or MAE in the units of $y$. Choose the threshold from the cost of each mistake. Use k-fold (stratified for classes) cross-validation when data are scarce, and still touch the test set once.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: The forward pass: layers as matrix multiplies
md: Keep the cached values. The forward pass is not just for the prediction: the backward pass will reuse every $z^l$ and $a^l$ computed here, so frameworks store them.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Training a real network: an MLP on handwritten digits
md: Use the test set once. If you pick the number of epochs, the learning rate or the hidden size by looking at test accuracy, the test set has become a validation set and its score is no longer an honest estimate. Choose with the validation set, then report test.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
md: "It is a single line of C" does not make it atomic, and `volatile` does not either: that C keyword only tells the compiler to really load and store the variable on every access instead of keeping it in a register. OSTEP's counter is declared `volatile int` and still loses updates.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Crash consistency: fsck and journaling
md: Write the pointed-to object before the object that points to it, and make the commit a single atomic write. Journaling turns three unordered writes into one all-or-nothing transaction, and recovery only has to read the log, not the whole disk.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Joint and marginal distributions, and the chain rule of probability
md: The joint table holds everything. Marginals are its row and column sums, conditionals are a row or column divided by its total, and the chain rule rebuilds the joint from one-variable conditionals.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL divergence
md: Entropy is average surprise under the truth, cross-entropy is average surprise under your model, and KL divergence is the gap. Training on cross-entropy minimizes KL from the data, which is maximum likelihood.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Counting training compute: C is about 6ND
md: 6ND counts useful model FLOPs, not wall-clock. Real hardware sustains only a fraction of its peak, so time and cost depend on utilization. And at long context lengths the attention term that 6N ignores stops being small. Serving a trained model costs about $2N$ FLOPs per generated token (forward pass only), which matters in lesson 7.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: Relevance is judged against the **information need**, not the query words. A document that contains every query term can still be nonrelevant, and a document with none of them can be relevant. That is exactly why judgments must come from people and not from term matching.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: A bi-encoder trades accuracy for speed in one specific way: the passage vector cannot look at the query. In exchange, every passage is encoded once, ahead of time, and search becomes a nearest-neighbor lookup among vectors. Everything else in this course follows from that trade.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A token is not a word. In GPT-2, " hello" (with its leading space) and "hello" are two different tokens with different ids, and many common words are split. Counting words is a poor estimate of token count.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Special tokens, chat templates and prompt boundaries
md: Special tokens are added by hand and matched before BPE, so only text you control should be allowed to produce them. Chat templates are just strings of special tokens and text. And the model sees ids, so prompt edges and spelling tasks inherit tokenization's boundaries.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
md: BatchNorm and Dropout behave **differently in train and eval mode**. `model.train()` and `model.eval()` flip that switch for every such layer at once; forgetting either one is among the most common silent bugs in practice.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Greedy search on a proximity graph, and why ef matters
md: Greedy graph search has no guarantee of exactness on a real (non-Delaunay) graph. Even a large $ef$ can miss a neighbor if the graph has no path that improves toward it. Recall comes from how well the graph is built, which is the subject of the next two lessons.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Protestware: when the legitimate maintainer is the threat
md: Misconception: "Signed packages are safe packages." A signature answers 'did this come from the expected publisher, unmodified?'. It cannot answer 'does the publisher mean well?'. Protestware, and the xz backdoor (a trusted maintainer by then), passed every authenticity check.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: The Gaussian loop: unbiased fits that still shrink to a point
md: Sampling error makes each generation's fit a random step, and steps that multiply variance by a mean-one factor still shrink it in the typical run. Unbiased estimation does not save a closed loop.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What happens when your program calls write
md: Two traps in the convention. The 4th argument goes in `r10`, not `rcx` as in a normal C call, because the `syscall` instruction itself overwrites `rcx` with the return address. And after the call, `rcx` and `r11` are garbage from your point of view. Compilers know this; hand-written inline assembly must list them as clobbered.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Editing the map: munmap, mprotect, mremap and how exec builds it
md: `munmap` can fail with `ENOMEM` even though it frees memory. mmap(2) explains why: unmapping a region in the middle of a mapping creates two smaller mappings, and that can exceed the per-process limit.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Why the average hides the requests users remember
md: Report latency as a distribution: several percentiles (p50, p99, p99.9) plus the maximum, not a mean. The mean blends a few terrible requests into many good ones and describes no actual user.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Allen relations, current roles and time-scoped queries
md: Every time-scoped question becomes interval arithmetic once two things are fixed: the reference date, and the convention for partial dates. Allen relations, current-role tests and window clipping are all a few endpoint comparisons.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Search against a PRM, revisions, and compute-optimal allocation
md: The best use of test-time compute depends on the prompt. Search is most valuable where the model is weak but not hopeless; on easy prompts it can hurt by exploiting the verifier.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Titans: surprise, momentum and a forget gate for neural memory
md: Titans' memory update = gradient descent with momentum (carry surprise forward) and weight decay (forget), all gated per token. Momentum keeps writing after a surprising event; forgetting keeps a fixed-size memory from overflowing.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Sizing M, filling the depot, and the memory you pay
md: A per-CPU or per-thread cache is a deliberate trade of memory for scalability. Idle rounds look like a leak in heap profiles and in RSS (resident set size, the physical memory a process currently holds), and they multiply by the number of CPUs (or threads) and caches. Every production design pairs its caches with a sizing policy and a way to give memory back.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: From hunt to detection: the FireEye countermeasures
md: Hunts and detections are two ends of one pipeline. Precise, low-volume hunts become alerts; noisy but valuable ones become scheduled hunts with an owner and a review rhythm, like FireEye's supplemental rules. A hunt that never feeds detection leaves the organisation exactly as blind as before, once the hunter moves on.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: The Diamond Model: one event, four corners
md: Two traps. First, Type 2 infrastructure is what victims usually see, so an IP address's owner is often another victim, not the adversary. Second, a shared feature is a lead, not a link: two events that share a widely used tool are not necessarily the same adversary (the attribution lesson returns to this).

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Assets and adversaries: what is worth taking, and by whom
md: Do not let one view take over. The Threat Modeling Manifesto lists *tendency to overfocus* as an anti-pattern: avoid exaggerating attention on adversaries, assets, or techniques. A model built only around a feared attacker misses dull, likely failures.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Case: Target 2013, a vendor login across a trust boundary
md: Compliance is not security. The Senate timeline notes that Target was certified compliant with PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, the card industry's security rules) in September 2013, two months before the breach. An audit checks controls at a moment; a threat model asks how an attacker would get from here to there.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Forecasting is supervised learning where the future is off limits
md: A random train/test split on a time series leaks the future into training and makes every model look better than it will be in production. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos state the rule plainly: the training set may contain only observations that occurred before the test observations, so no future observations are used to construct the forecast.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Downgrade attacks: POODLE, BEAST, Logjam and the fixes
md: Downgrade defence has two halves: **authenticate the negotiation** (transcript signatures, the sentinel, SCSV) and **delete the weak options** so there is nothing to downgrade to. The second is the one that always works.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
md: A Triton program instance is not one thread. It is closer to a CUDA thread block: one program becomes `num_warps` warps of 32 threads each, so with the default `num_warps=4` a single program runs on 128 threads.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Attention masks for mixed text and image sequences
md: The rule that keeps any mask honest: a position may only attend to what will exist when it is generated. Bidirectional attention inside an image is legal exactly when the whole image is produced together, as in diffusion, flow or masked prediction. Under token-by-token generation it would leak the answer.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Syscalls become function calls: one address space, one privilege level
md: Running an unmodified binary on a unikernel does not get you function-call costs. Trapping and translating each `syscall` cost 84 cycles in Unikraft's measurement, 21 times a function call. Relinking against the libOS is what removes the crossing.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: The spectrum: Linux-based unikernels, microVMs and sandboxes
md: Unikernel gains split into **removing the crossing** (small for real applications, per Lupine) and **specializing** (large). Linux can deliver much of the second. Choose a libOS unikernel when you also want tiny images, millisecond boots and a minimal attack surface, and can accept its limits.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
md: Durability comes from the log, not the index: indexes are rebuilt or replayed from the WAL. Speed comes from what fits in RAM: keep the navigation data (graph upper layers, compressed vectors) in memory, and make every disk read count.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and running verl in practice
md: verl in one sentence: a single Python controller expresses the RL algorithm as calls on WorkerGroups; each WorkerGroup runs a training or inference engine SPMD on a resource pool; DataProto carries the batch between them; and actor and rollout share GPUs by resharding or sleeping instead of keeping two copies.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Measuring world models, and where Genie 2 and 3 go next
md: A video world model is three choices: how frames become latents (VQ tokens or continuous), how actions enter (logged, learned latent codes, or text), and how the next frame is sampled (masked token decoding or diffusion). All of them pay for autoregression with drift and finite memory, and they are judged on fidelity (FVD, human studies) and on control (delta PSNR).

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
md: A VLA is a VLM whose output vocabulary also contains actions. Predicting the robot's next move becomes one more question the model answers, so the whole web-pretrained network is reused for control.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
md: Track usage and perplexity during tokenizer training. A 16,384-entry codebook with perplexity 500 behaves like a much smaller vocabulary and wastes embedding rows in every downstream model.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
md: Graph capture assumes `forward` does the same thing at replay as at capture. That is why `AttentionImpl.forward` must not branch on Python values that change per batch inside a full graph, and why builders write into persistent buffers instead of allocating new tensors.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Reading a receipt into validated JSON
md: Do not ask the model to fill in a missing total by computing it. Then the arithmetic check compares the model with itself and can never fail.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
md: Two checks in `help_enq` look redundant but are not. The paper shows that replacing `while (isStillPending(tid, phase))` with `while (true)` breaks wait-freedom, and dropping the second `isStillPending` check just before the CAS on `last.next` breaks linearizability, because a thread that was suspended there could insert a node another helper already inserted.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Foundation models, hybrids, and where these models break
md: "Foundation model" here does not mean a chatbot for weather. It means one pretrained network whose weights are reused and fine-tuned across forecasting tasks.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Testing authorization at scale: two accounts and a replay matrix
md: If a replay ever returns another person's real data, stop. Do not page through more records to measure the scale. The disclose.io terms ask researchers to limit data access to the minimum needed for a proof of concept and to cease testing and report immediately when they encounter user data.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: How a page loads: HTML, subresources, JavaScript and the DOM
md: A script runs with the authority of **the page that includes it**, not the server it came from. `lib.js` from `cdn.example.net` runs as if `shop.example.com` had written it: it can read and change the shop's DOM, read the shop's visible cookies and send requests to the shop with the user's cookies. Including a script is handing over your keys.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Subresource Integrity and the trust you hand to third-party scripts
md: SRI only works for files that never change between requests. It cannot pin a script that is generated per request or a library loaded as "latest". Pin exact versions, self-host what you can, and keep the list of third-party scripts on sensitive pages (login, payment) as short as possible.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event IDs that tell an intrusion story: 4688, 4720, 7045, 1102
md: Turn on command-line logging for 4688 (or deploy Sysmon). Without it you know rundll32.exe ran, but not what it was told to do, and that is usually the part that matters.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Rogue access points, evil twins and how enterprises find them
md: An evil twin of an *open* network is indistinguishable from the real one at the Wi-Fi layer: there is nothing to authenticate. Users on open or OWE networks must rely on TLS (lesson 9) for everything that matters.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Lockdown Mode, stalkerware and tracker abuse
md: For someone being monitored by an abuser, every defensive step can also alert the abuser: monitoring stopping, a tracker going silent. Technical help here should follow the person's own safety plan, ideally with a domestic violence support service, not just maximise security.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Run it yourself: one stable trunk, three cooldown branches
md: Branch checklist: weights, optimizer state (including its step count), the global step that drives the LR schedule, and the data position. A loss spike on the first step of a branch means the optimizer state was not restored; a branch that starts with a warmup means the step counter was reset.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely
md: A notification means "the kernel has released your pages", **not** "the data was delivered". With a deferred copy it can arrive before the copied data is even transmitted. Never use it as a transmit or delivery acknowledgement.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Evaluating zero-shot classifiers and choosing thresholds
md: The perfect F1 at 0.6 comes from 12 decisions on 3 hand-picked texts. A threshold tuned on so few examples is overfit. Use hundreds of labeled examples, and keep a separate test split to report the final number.
